name: Berlin Blue
lede: Berlin blue is the German name of an early synthetic blue pigment, better known as Prussian blue, and in Werner's mineral colors it is the plate with the jay's wing and the blue sapphire.

sections.title: A name that outlived its place
sections.body:
Berlin blue is the older, German name of the iron-blue pigment that English speakers call [[prussian-blue]] [1]. Paterson's dictionary describes it as often the same as Prussian blue, but also as a lighter sapphire blue [1]. The name belongs to the city where the pigment was first sold, and it is one of many: Paterson also lists Chinese, Milori, Paris, iron and steel blue for the same family [1].

Books disagree on when the pigment was made. Paterson gives 1704 for its accidental creation in Berlin [1]. Pastoureau dates it between 1704 and 1707 in one book, and 1709 in another, where he credits the Berlin pharmacist Heinrich Diesbach [2][3]. Our library cites Maerz and Paul for the color word itself in 1724 [4].

sections.title: Diesbach, Dippel and the red that turned blue
sections.body:
Pastoureau tells it as an accident. Diesbach, a druggist and pigment maker, normally sold a red lake made from cochineal, iron sulfate and potassium, and one day he ran out of potassium [2]. He bought some from Johann Konrad Dippel, who sold him an adulterated potassium carbonate, and the batch came out a magnificent blue [2].

Dippel saw the profit at once. He worked out that the impure potassium had caused the blue, refined the process, and sold the color as Berlin blue [2]. For more than a decade he kept the recipe secret, and he made a considerable fortune before the English chemist M. D. Woodward published the composition in 1724 [2]. Pastoureau adds that Dippel later left Berlin ruined and became doctor to the Swedish king Frederick I [2].

sections.title: What German color books meant
sections.body:
In nineteenth-century German writing on pigments, Berlin blue was the common term and Prussian blue was not [5]. Gentele (1860), Bouvier (1861) and Rose (1916) all favor Berlin blue as the main name [5]. The Pigment Compendium says the terminology of Berlin, Paris and Prussian blue was variable in these sources, though particular texts show particular relations [5].

Some writers drew lines. Linke and Adam (1913) call Berlin blue a lighter form of Paris blue, mixed with other substances [5]. Schulze (1826) says that leaving out alum made a darker blue, which he called Paris blue [5]. Gentele says that for economy Berlin blue was made by mixing Paris blue with starch, baryte, calcium sulfate, or burnt clay and kaolin [5]. Terry (1893) used Paris blue for the violet-tinted kind of Prussian blue [6].

Mierzinski (1881) used the term mineral blue for a pale Berlin blue containing zinc oxide [7]. Salter lists Berlin blue among the terms linked to Antwerp blue, a zinc form of the same pigment family [7].

The paint trade used Berlin blue as an ingredient [8]. Mierzinski gives a bluish white of one part Berlin blue to 140 parts white, and one kind of commercial sky blue was lead or zinc white tinted with it [8]. His bronze green is chrome yellow, zinc white, Berlin blue and black, and green cinnabar, a synonym of chrome green, was chrome yellow mixed with Paris blue or Berlin blue [9].

sections.title: Werner's Berlin Blue
sections.body:
In mineralogy the name took on a second life. Abraham Werner's color nomenclature, as revised by Patrick Syme in 1821, lists both Prussian Blue and Berlin Blue as separate entries, no. 31 being Berlin Blue [12][11]. Baty notes that the two names are interchangeable in theory, yet Syme uses both [12].

Syme's example for Berlin Blue is the wing feathers of a jay, the flower of the hepatica, and, among minerals, [[gem:sapphire|blue sapphire]] [11]. Baty calls it the pure, characteristic color of Werner [11]. Syme also treated it as a building block. For his Flax-flower Blue the recipe is Berlin blue plus a slight tinge of ultramarine; Verditter Blue adds a little verdigris green; Greenish Blue adds white and some emerald green [11][12]. Even his whites were tinted with it: Skimmed-milk White contains a little Berlin blue and ash grey [12].

The swatch on this page is Werner's no. 31 as scanned from an aged plate, carried through Ridgway's 1886 and 1912 color books into our library [4].

sections.title: In painting and print
sections.body:
As Prussian blue, the pigment turned up in the skies of Canaletto and Gainsborough, according to Paterson [1]. Pastoureau says its coloring power was very strong, that in mixtures it gave clear tones, and that painters in England, Germany and the north used it more than painters in France or Italy [3]. In Japan the pigment became *bero*, from the Dutch for Berlin blue [13].

Paterson lists it as one of the first synthetic pigments [1]. The Pigment Compendium names a long list of variants for the family, from American blue and Haarlem blue to Hamburg blue and Erlangen blue [10].

sections.title: The swatch is not the pigment
sections.body: The color on this page is light and greyed: Werner's plate, scanned, reads as a pale blue with a lightness of about 60 and little chroma [4]. The pigment itself is a very deep blue, and our Prussian Blue swatch is #003153 [4]. ISCC-NBS 1955 calls the nearest block a "light purplish blue" at a distance of about 7 CIEDE2000 units [4]. Syme's list treats Berlin Blue as a pale cousin of his darker Prussian Blue, and the swatch should be read as that [12][4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, as photographed, 189 hold this blue (within CIEDE2000 6) over at least 5 per cent of the canvas [14]. The largest shares are [[painting:aic-28290|Portrait of Prince Azam Shah]], about 1660, at 51 per cent, and Frans Post's [[painting:smk-KMSsp491|Landscape in Brazil with Sugar Plantation]], 1660, at 42 per cent [14]. Sisley's [[painting:commons-Q17493189|The Bridge at Moret]], 1893, reaches 30 per cent [14].

The match is strongest among landscape painters. [[painter:claude-monet|Monet]] has it in 5 of his 50 works here, Sisley and Lundbye in 4 each, and Impressionism as a group in 6 of 140 paintings [14]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 39 per cent of the 147 paintings where it is found, as ranked by lightness within each painting [15]. Its companions are [[cornflower]], [[steel-blue]] and [[slate]] [14].

The earliest match is Dieric Bouts's *Nativity*, 1445, at 6 per cent [14]. That is more than 250 years before the pigment and 376 years before Werner's swatch, so this is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph and not proof of the pigment or dye [14][4].

openers: German chemists mostly called Prussian blue 'Berlin blue'; paint makers also used it to whiten and to mix cheap greens.
Syme tinted whites with Berlin blue: his Skimmed-milk White contains a little of it.
Look for the jay's wing: Werner's Berlin Blue is the bird's feathers, hepatica and blue sapphire.
